newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa party says it is ready to join government.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa party says it is ready to join government.

text.p: South Africa's small Pan Africanist Congress said on Wednesday it was ready to accept President Nelson Mandela's offer to join his government of national unity.
"We have accepted in principle participation in the government," Stanley Mogoba, the party's new president, told reporters after meeting Mandela at the president's Johannesburg home. No time was set.
Mandela and Mogoba said they would consult their parties and meet again to work out a deal.
"I don't think it is proper for us to waste our energies as democratic forces by keeping ourselves divided," Mandela said after the meeting.

Mandela's coalition cabinet includes the mainly Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party, but the National Party of former president F.W. de Klerk pulled out last year, saying the country could benefit from a robust opposition.

The PAC fought apartheid with the slogan "one (white) settler, one bullet" but its radical leftist platform failed to appeal to voters and it fared miserably in the 1994 democratic elections that brought Mandela to power.
Mandela's African National Congress won just under two-thirds of the vote, ensuring it a dominant role in power.

Although the PAC failed to win the five percent vote needed to secure it a place in the unity government, Mandela offered to bring it in, but party boss Clarence Makwetu, who stood down in December, rejected it.
Some commentators say joining the government will be disastrous for the PAC, which will be forced to go along with the wishes of the ANC.

The PAC campaigned mainly on a black supremacist platform and a demand for the return of land taken from blacks since the first white settlers arrived in 1652. It won only five of the 400 parliamentary seats, with 1.25 percent of the vote.
Mogoba stepped down last month as head of the Methodist Church in South Africa, which counts Mandela among its members, to lead the PAC, which he said needed him.

The party was founded in 1959 by ANC members dissatisfied with the high-profile role of whites in the movement and with the party's alliance with other groups, including the South African Communist Party.
